newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Hope outweighs fear as N.Korean defector flies out.
newsitem.headline: Hope outweighs fear as N.Korean defector flies out.

text.p: The flight to freedom of Pyongyang's top ideologue on Tuesday is unlikely to spark new inter-Korean tensions, analysts said, but the cloak-and-dagger operation underscores fears of retaliation.

Asian nations are still haunted by memories of the 1983 Rangoon bombing, when North Korean agents blew up 12 members of a South Korean government delegation, including four ministers, in the Burmese capital.

Such memories account for the secrecy shrouding Hwang Jang-yop's passage from Seoul's diplomatic mission in Beijing to the Philippines, where military officers said he was ensconced in a remote mountain resort.
But analysts in Seoul said North Korea was now desperate for food aid, and unlikely to risk jeopardising Western grain supplies by lashing out.

Overcoming the food crisis was more important to North Korea than settling scores with Seoul, particularly as Pyongyang's government prepared for the formal accession to power of top leader Kim Jong-il, the analysts said.
"North Korea is now preoccupied with food aid it needs to stave off famine," said Lee Seo-hang, a fellow at the Institute of Foreign Affairs and National Security run by the Seoul foreign ministry.
"We don't expect Hwang's defection to have any major impact on our relation with the North," Deputy National Unification Minister Lee Ho told Reuters.
But analysts cautioned that any attempt by Seoul to score propaganda points by parading Hwang once he got to South Korea could result in a flare-up of tensions between the Koreas.
A South Korean foreign ministry spokesman on Tuesday said that by letting Hwang go, Beijing had acted in accordance with international norms. Nevertheless, it was an agonising choice for China.
China eventually come down on the side of wealthy investment partner Seoul, highlighting a widening gulf between Beijing and its old ideological comrade Pyongyang, the political analysts said.
"China will be increasingly driven by economic pragmatism," said Lee Seo-hang.

"China has remained a key player on the Korean peninsula and does not want to lose influence over the North altogether. But its policy would be decided by self-interest and economic ties will take on more importance," he said.
While China once described its ties with North Korea as being "as close as lips and teeth", it took no security chances during Hwang's five weeks in South Korea's consulate in the Chinese capital.
Armed Chinese police guarded the compound and several armoured personnel carriers were parked nearby. Rolls of spikes blocked approaches to the mission.
Extra security was clamped on flights from Beijing to South Korea. Long queues formed as passengers bound for Seoul were subjected to full body-searches.
Lee Seo-hang speculated that a secret food deal for North Korea may have clinched agreement for Hwang's departure.
"South Korea must have assured China it wanted to help relieve food shorages in North Korea, probably through the four-nation peace talks," Lee said.
He was referring to proposed talks involving both Koreas, the United States and China to thrash out a peace mechanism to replace a truce that ended the 1950-1953 Korean War.
North Korea raised hopes it would join the talks after its officials attended a briefing this month by the United States and South Korea.
Deputy minister Lee said Pyongyang's participation in the New York briefing "clearly reflects how desperate North Korea has become and how serious North Korea's difficulties are".

The World Food Programme (WFP) said North Korea faced a shortfall of 1.7 million tonnes of grain this year, even after its own imports of 500,000 tonnes and WFP aid of 100,000 tonnes were taken into account.

Diplomats in Beijing said Hwang's detour through the Philippines would help Pyongyang save face while reassuring Seoul its prize catch would be out of easy reach of Northern agents. North Korea does not have an embassy in the Philippines.
"They want to be able to present it somehow for internal consumption as not having been a straightforward defection to South Korea," said one Beijing-based envoy.
"Obviously the defection was a blow, but they haven't been humiliated any further as a result."
